record.title: Oral History Interview with Stanley Cloud

point.title: Introduction
point.partial_transcript: So hello, everyone. My name is Jack Zipper. Today is April 4th, 2026.
point.synopsis: Jack Zipper begins the interview and introduces the narrator, Stanley Cloud.

point.title: Early Life and Military Service
point.partial_transcript: Yeah, so let's get started. So where and when were you born?
point.synopsis: Cloud discusses his early life and education in California. Born in Los Angeles, Cloud studied at Pepperdine College, where he majored in English. He then entered the Navy, where he first attended the Officer Candidate School and served on two destroyers in the Pacific Ocean as a gunnery officer. During his career, he attended language school in Monterey, where he learned Russian.
point.keywords: Navy; Pepperdine College; Russian; Monterey; California; Los Angeles; Officer Candidate School

point.title: Early Journalism and Tenure at Time San Francisco
point.partial_transcript: Oh, interesting. We'll get there. So how did you exit the Navy to then get into journalism?
point.synopsis: After leaving the Navy, Cloud joined the Monterey Herald and covered the county government. He ended up transitioning to Time in 1968, where he covered San Francisco and the events in the city. Cloud also discusses how his passion from journalism came from his grandfather, who was the editor of a small newspaper in Kansas. He describes his choice to become a journalist as a "natural thing for [him] to do."
point.keywords: Monterey; Monterey Herald; Time; Time Magazine; San Francisco; Journalism; California

point.title: Tenure in Moscow and Transition to Bangkok / Opinions of the Vietnam War
point.partial_transcript: Okay. So then, let's go back a little bit before we get to that. So you're going to Moscow. What did you cover there, and what was that like?
point.synopsis: Cloud describes his time as a correspondent in the Moscow Bureau for Time Magazine and his move to Bangkok after he was kicked out of the country in April of 1970. He also shares his opinions of the Vietnam War prior to his arrival in Bangkok. He shared that he was against the war and thought it was a mistake. Cloud also discusses, when he became a reporter for Time initially, how he had his doubts about Time's pro-war stance. However, he believes that the elevation of Henry [A.] Grunwald to managing editor helped Time become a less biased and more respectable publication.
point.keywords: Vietnam War; Vietnam; Bangkok; Moscow; Russia; Thailand; Journalism; Time; Time Magazine

point.title: Technical Difficulties
point.synopsis: The interview encounters some technical difficulties. Cloud and Zipper attempt to find a solution.

point.title: Role of Bureau Chief in Bangkok
point.partial_transcript: Okay. So we're resuming this interview after some technical difficulties.
point.synopsis: The interview resumes after technical difficulties. Cloud discusses his time as Bureau Chief in Bangkok from 1970-71, where he covered the wars in Cambodia and Laos. He discusses the differences between the wars in Cambodia and Laos and the war in Vietnam. Cloud mentions that Time as a publication had become less pro-war, so he as bureau chief did not feel pressure from Time to position their stories in a certain way. Cloud recounts his harrowing adventure in Prey Totueng, a town northeast of Phnom Penh, where he and a freelance photographer he knew were trapped in an active battle and pinned by sniper fire. Cloud describes his time in Bangkok as great and that he had a lot of fun.
point.keywords: Bangkok; Cambodia; Laos; Thailand; Prey Totueng; Phnom Penh; journalism; Vietnam; Vietnam War

point.title: Initial Meeting and First Impressions of Pham Xuan An
point.partial_transcript: So being a bureau chief, what did that mean to work with the other correspondents? Were you managing them?
point.synopsis: Cloud describes his first first impressions of Pham Xuan An upon meeting him, how he and others in the bureau interacted with An, and An's habits around the office. An was a valuable resource for Cloud for information on stories, and Cloud and Time writers would often go to An to get his thoughts. Cloud also gives a brief overview of his responsibilities as bureau chief. There is a brief technical glitch/interruption.
point.keywords: Pham Xuan An; Time; Saigon; Vietnam; Vietnam War; journalism

point.title: Discussions of the War with An
point.partial_transcript: During your tenure, did you ever have conversations with him about the war?
point.synopsis: Cloud discusses his conversations with An about An's opinions on the Vietnam War. Cloud recounts that An believed the war was a mistake. However, Cloud did not get into many philosophical conversations about the war. In addition, Cloud recalls that An had connections to famous U.S. spies like Edward G. Lansdale, and that Time was the envy of the other bureaus in Vietnam for having An on their staff. Cloud describes how he felt "depressed" about the trajectory of the war and the lasting impact it had on the Vietnamese.
point.keywords: Pham Xuan An; Vietnam; Vietnam War; Time; Edward Landsdale; Spy; Journalism

point.title: Impactful Stories and An's contribution
point.partial_transcript: And what were some of those stories that you covered during the war that you felt like really were impactful?
point.synopsis: Cloud discusses some of the big stories he worked on during his tenure as Bureau Chief. A big story he worked on was the Easter Offensive, where he would sit down with An every week to discuss the developments and get An's thoughts. Cloud remembers that An would often tell anecdotes that helped frame the context of the historical situation, and that all of the information he received from An held up to the historical record and could not have been interpreted as bias. Conversations with An, and An's wisdom and integrity, helped Cloud develop an innate feel for the war, and he says it was a joy to talk to him. Cloud recounts how An saw himself as an analyst.
point.keywords: Pham Xuan An; Easter Offensive; Vietnam; Vietnam War; Time; Journalism

point.title: An's Qualities / Discussion of World Memo
point.partial_transcript: And now at that time, I read a 2015 Time article that includes a 1972 memo written around this time of the Easter Offensive.
point.synopsis: Cloud describes the qualities of An that stood out. Cloud recalls that had a great sense humor and deep historical understanding of Vietnam that far surpassed most Americans at that time. There is also a discussion about a memo that Cloud wrote about An, but Cloud also does not remember writing it.
point.keywords: Time; Memo; Pham Xuan An; Journalism; Vietnam; Vietnam War

point.title: Departure from Saigon and Work in Washington D.C.
point.partial_transcript: No. That's totally fine. We could definitely move on. So then—so in 1972, that's the tail end of your time at the bureau in Saigon. So when did you leave Saigon?
point.synopsis: Cloud discusses his transition to Washington D.C., where he served as a Senate correspondent for Time before working his way up to the bureau chief of the Washington D.C. bureau. Cloud recalls that his experience in Vietnam made him more distrustful of the government and skeptical of their decisions, but that his perspective did not influence his reporting.

point.title: Reaction to News of An Being a Spy
point.partial_transcript: Got it. So then you make your way up to being the bureau chief.
point.synopsis: Cloud discusses his reactions to the discovery of An's career as a spy. He describes his reaction as stunned, but understood where An was coming from. He also discusses the reactions of his fellow colleagues at Time and in the general journalism community; while some felt betrayed by An, most also understood and were not critical of his actions.
point.keywords: Time; Spy; Pham Xuan An; Discovery; Journalism

point.title: Visits to Vietnam
point.partial_transcript: Now that you know that An was a spy, were there any moments or things that you saw from An that may have been him actually practicing his spy craft?
point.synopsis: Cloud recounts his visits to Vietnam in the 1990s, where he saw An. He remembers visiting An that first time was like "time hadn't passed," and they shared about how things were. Cloud recalled that An was not fond of the new presence of communist regime and the Russians that had occurred in Vietnam after the end of the war. Cloud felt that his visits to Vietnam were uplifting, and he sensed pride from the Vietnamese people. Cloud also recalls An's sense of humor. He does not remember, during his time in Vietnam, any time that he could have seen An practicing his spycraft.
point.keywords: Vietnam; Vietnam War; Pham Xuan An; Russian

point.title: An's Love for Vietnam / An's Family
point.partial_transcript: Why do you think An disliked the regime?
point.synopsis: Cloud discusses how the regime often conflicted with An's laid back, which stemmed from his life in South Vietnam, attitude. Cloud shares that An had a deep love for Vietnam, one that surpassed his allegiance to the communist regime. Cloud also shares about his relationship with An's family and his conversations with An's wife, Thu Nhan, about her uncertainty when returning to Vietnam from the United States.
point.keywords: Pham Xuan An; Vietnam; Communism; Thu Nhan

point.title: An's Trust in Others / Fundraising for An Pham
point.partial_transcript: That's interesting. Do you think because he didn't know who to trust, that puts him in a pretty awkward position?
point.synopsis: Cloud discusses how An maintained relations with all sides of the Vietnam War, including Americans and the Vietnamese. Cloud believes that An trusted in him and other American journalists. He also discusses his contribution to the fundraising for the An Pham's college studies, An's son, where he wrote a check to help An Pham study in North Carolina.
point.keywords: Trust; Pham Xuan An; Vietnam; Vietnam War; Journalism; Saigon; Journalist; American; An Pham; North Carolina; fundraising

point.title: Reflections and Concluding Thoughts on Vietnam and An
point.partial_transcript: So then looking back at your relationship with An. What do you think An has taught you?
point.synopsis: Cloud offers his concluding thoughts about Pham Xuan An. He discusses how An helped him and how the Vietnam War made him a wiser person. He describes An as "unforgettable" and goes onto reflect on what made An special. He also says how he misses talking to An since he passed away. Cloud also discusses a memoir he is writing, which he describes as more of an autobiography. There is a whole chapter of the memoir on An.
point.keywords: Pham Xuan An; Memoir; Vietnam; Vietnam War; reflection

point.title: Outro and Goodbyes
point.partial_transcript: And do you have any other concluding thoughts about our conversation today?
point.synopsis: Cloud and Zipper say their goodbyes and conclude the interview
